newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - CENFED CEO seeks acquisitions.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - CENFED CEO seeks acquisitions.

text.p: CENFED Financial Corp president and chief executive officer Tad Lowrey said he expects to participate on the buy side of the current West Coast banking consolidation.
"We see ourselves as a buyer, not a seller," Lowrey told Reuters in an interview this week at the annual convention of the Western Savings Institutions in Santa Barbara.
"Our goal is not to sell. We realize in this marketplace there will be a lot of deals. I don't think we'll close any in 1996, but we've been been actively talking," he said.

CENFED, a thrift with about $2.1 billion in assets, is often named among the list of California takeover candidates following this year's spate of bank mergers, including Wells Fargo and Co's purchase of First Interstate Bancorp Inc, Washington Mutual Savings Bank's acquisition of American Savings Bank of Irvine and First Nationwide Bank's merger with California Federal Bancorp Inc.
"WAMU and First Nationwide are most likely buyers of additional thrifts in California, but they'll be pretty tied up in the next six to nine months, absorbing their recent acquisitions," Lowrey said.
While Lowrey said he prefers to participate on the buy side, he felt that he would be obligated to succumb to a takeover offer if it benefitted CENFED's shareholders.

CENFED nearly tripled its earnings to $4.3 million in the first quarter, compared with $1.6 million in the year-ago period. In the second quarter, it earned $3 million or $0.59 a share, up from $1.3 million or $0.27 a share in the year-ago period.
Lowrey said that CENFED has expanded through three aquisitions in the past four years. He declined to say with which companies CENFED had recently discussed deals.
"Several deals did not work out, based on our internal models. Some of these companies sold to other companies for more," he said, adding, "a company is worth different prices to different sellers."
Lowrey said CENFED would hope to acquire a specialty lender, with a focus in a niche market. It would also consider buying a thrift, commercial bank or a deposit franchise.
"I think we'll see more thrifts getting together as they face more shareholder demands to increase returns and save costs," he said, adding, "It will improve their franchises."
